newsitem.title: INDIA: Lower Indian rates seen unlikely to last long.
newsitem.headline: Lower Indian rates seen unlikely to last long.

text.p: India's central bank and Finance Minister P.Chidambaram, whose minority government fell on Friday, want lower interest rates to fuel a flagging economy but any cuts are unlikely to last long, analysts said.
The Reserve Bank of India releases a half year credit policy statement on Tuesday which is likely to contain measures which will prompt banks to cut rates and help credit expansion.
Leading state-run banks currently charge their best borrowers between 14 and 14.5 percent.
"They may come down a half-point, there is not much further leeway," Rajan Govil, economist for James Capel B&K brokerage, told Reuters.

Domestic price rises, unplanned monetisation of the government deficit -- effectively printing money -- and other upward pressure on monetary growth would feed inflation, preventing the RBI from allowing any easing to continue for long, analysts said.
"Something has got to give and it's undoubtedly going to be interest rates," said Mark McFarland, senior economist at Peregrine Brokerage Ltd in Hong Kong.
Keeping inflation in single digits would require the central bank to reverse the downtrend in rates in the second half of fiscal 1997/98 (April-March), analysts said.
"Interest rates will probably go up within the next year," McFarland said.
"Inflation is kicking up," he added, citing increased domestic coal prices and expected hikes in petroleum product prices as two factors pressuring inflation.

Inflation, measured by the wholesale price index, was 7.35 percent year-on-year in the last week of March, compared with 5.01 percent a year ago. RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan wants it between five and seven percent.
NatWest Securities in Bombay is forecasting an average for fiscal 1997/98 of 8.2 percent. Capel's Govil expects inflation to clock nine percent over the next year.
NatWest predicted interest rates would be depressed by excess liquidity through the first half of the fiscal year, but would be pressured higher in the second half.
In a report issued on Friday it said the prime lending rate was likely to rise more than inflation, so real interest rates would rise in the second half.
"However, average real interest rates in FY98 will be lower than in FY97," the research report said.

But now the onus is on the RBI to keep the recovery moving and produce a credit environment that fits in with Chidambaram's 1997/98 budget, which will be debated in parliament on April 21-23 despite the fall of the United Front government.
The tax cutting, business friendly budget aimed to give India's economic growth much-needed extra momentum and breathe fresh life into the country's liberalisation efforts.
Lack of confidence and complaints from business that interest rates are too high have dogged the recovery.
Rangarajan has said he believed the RBI's 16 percent target for M3 growth provided ample room for meeting credit demand from the government and companies.
But NatWest said government borrowings higher than the budget factored in and would lead to higher interest rates.

"Though the budget provides only for an increase of 15 billion rupees in the government's market borrowings, we feel that the budget's revenue targets might be over-optimistic by about 50 billon rupees," it said.
To prompt banks to cut prime lending rates, the RBI is expected to cut the maximum interest rate on bank deposits under one year from 10 percent to at least nine, bankers said.
Some newspapers have said the RBI might introduce a maximum rate of eight percent for deposits up to six months.
This would give banks extra room to cut prime lending rates and get Indian credit growth moving.
